a: The book of the family history
p: Matthew's first words echo Genesis: "the book of the family history of Adam."
b: Biblos geneseōs is the phrase the Septuagint (the Greek Old Testament made before Jesus) uses for Genesis 2:4, where its wording is "the book of the origin of heaven and earth," and for Genesis 5:1, "This is the book of the family history of Adam." Genesis can mean birth, origin, family line or life story. So the opening line may title only the family list (1:2–17), the birth story too (the same word returns in 1:18, "beginning"), or the whole Gospel, as a "book of the new genesis" brought by Jesus. Many readers think Matthew means all three at once: a new start for humanity, as the first book of the Bible began the first.

p: "Jesus" is Hebrew Yeshua, "the LORD saves." "Christ" is Greek for Messiah, "anointed one."
b: Iēsous is the Greek form of Yeshua (Joshua), a common Jewish name meaning "the LORD saves" (see 1:21). Christos translates the Hebrew mashiach, "anointed one," the title of Israel's kings and priests, and in Jesus' time the hoped-for king of David's line. Here, without "the," it is part of a name, so this translation writes "Jesus Christ." Where Matthew writes "the Christ" as a title (1:17; 2:4; 16:16), the Plain English Translation says "the Messiah," so readers can see the claim being made.

a: son of David, son of Abraham
p: David received the promise of an everlasting king; Abraham, the promise of blessing for all nations.
b: Matthew names the two men God made lasting promises to. To David God promised, "Your throne will stand firm for all time" (2 Samuel 7:16), and "son of David" was a title for the coming king (Psalms of Solomon 17:21). To Abraham God promised, "All the clans of the earth will find blessing in you" (Genesis 12:3). The order matters: Matthew tells first of the king sent to Israel (10:6; 15:24), and he ends with the risen Jesus sending his followers to "all nations" (28:19). Gentiles appear early, too: the women of the family list and the magi from the east.

p: The same verb runs 39 times through the list, and it does not always mean a direct father.
b: Egennēsen, "fathered" or "became the father of," is the KJV's "begat." In Bible family lists it can skip generations: a man "fathers" a grandson or a later descendant, as 1:8 and 1:11 show (compare 1 Chronicles 3:11–12, 15–16). The steady rhythm, "A fathered B, B fathered C," is copied from lists such as Ruth 4:18–22 and 1 Chronicles 2. The pattern holds until 1:16, where Matthew changes it on purpose (see the note there).

t: Four women in a list of men
p: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Uriah's wife break the pattern. Why does Matthew name them?
b: Jewish family lists rarely named women, and Matthew skips Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah. Instead he names four women with unusual stories: Tamar, who posed as a prostitute to get justice from Judah (Genesis 38), Rahab of Jericho, Ruth the Moabite, and Bathsheba, "Uriah's wife." Readers explain them in several ways. Sinners shown grace (Jerome, Chrysostom): the Messiah came for sinners. Gentiles (Luther and many today): Rahab was a Canaanite and Tamar probably one (Genesis does not say), Ruth a Moabite, Bathsheba married to a Hittite, so the nations belong to Jesus' family from the start. Strange unions blessed by God (Raymond Brown and others): each relationship looked scandalous, yet God used it to carry on the line, and this prepares for Mary. Women who acted: each took bold steps that kept the line going. The views can be combined.
r: Genesis 38:6–30; Joshua 2:1–21; Joshua 6:25; Ruth 4:13–17; 2 Samuel 11:2–27; 1:16; Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25

p: The Old Testament never says whom Rahab married. Matthew alone links her to David's family.
b: Joshua 2 and 6 tell of Rahab, the woman of Jericho who hid Israel's spies, but say nothing of a husband. Ruth 4:21 and 1 Chronicles 2:11 name Salmon as Boaz's father, without his wife. No earlier source puts Rahab in David's line; a rabbinic tradition instead says she married Joshua (Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 14b). Some think Matthew knew a Jewish tradition now lost; others that he drew the link himself. Two other questions: the spelling Rhachab differs from the Septuagint's Raab, and the time from the conquest to David seems too long for four generations, so the list may again skip names.

p: Matthew names Uriah, not Bathsheba: a reminder of David's adultery and murder.
b: The Greek says only "from the [one] of Uriah." Matthew could have written "Bathsheba," but by naming her first husband he recalls 2 Samuel 11: David took another man's wife and had the husband killed. Uriah was a Hittite, a foreigner loyal to Israel, and Bathsheba may have been counted as his household. Even the greatest king in the line needed mercy. "David the king" stands at the turning point of the list: he is the only one Matthew calls king, and the line rises to him and falls after him.
orig: ἐκ τῆς τοῦ Οὐρίου (ek tēs tou Ouriou)

p: Between Joram and Uzziah, Kings and Chronicles list three more kings: Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah.
b: 1 Chronicles 3:11–12 runs "Joram his son, Ahaziah his son, Joash his son, Amaziah his son, Azariah his son," and Azariah is Uzziah (2 Kings 15:1, 13). Matthew skips three generations, and in 1:11 he skips Jehoiakim between Josiah and Jeconiah. For the count of fourteen: the list was shaped to make the pattern (1:17), and family lists often skipped names. A judgment: these three were descendants of Ahab and Jezebel through Athaliah (2 Kings 8:18, 26), and some ancient readers (Hilary, Jerome) linked the gap to the curse on Ahab's house. A copying slip: in Greek Ochozias (Ahaziah) and Ozias (Uzziah) look alike, so the eye may have jumped from one to the other.
r: 1 Chronicles 3:10–12; 2 Kings 8:16–27; 2 Kings 11:1–3; 2 Kings 14:1; 2 Kings 15:1; 2 Chronicles 22:1–4; 1:17

p: Jeconiah was Josiah's grandson, and Jeremiah said none of his children would sit on David's throne.
b: Jeconiah (also called Jehoiachin or Coniah) was the son of Jehoiakim, who was Josiah's son (1 Chronicles 3:15–16). He ruled three months before Nebuchadnezzar took him to Babylon in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:8–15). Jeremiah 22:30 declared that none of his offspring would sit on David's throne. A Jewish answer: the rabbis taught that exile atoned for Jeconiah and the decree was cancelled (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 37b–38a; Leviticus Rabbah 19:6; Pesikta de-Rav Kahana 24:11), and the Bible itself seems to reverse the curse when Haggai 2:23 calls his grandson Zerubbabel God's "signet ring" (compare Jeremiah 22:24). A Christian argument, common in modern evangelical apologetics (for example Arnold Fruchtenbaum): Jesus is Jeconiah's legal heir through Joseph but not his descendant by blood, so the curse does not touch him. Critics answer that by Matthew's own logic a legal heir inherits the line's standing. The "brothers" may stand for his uncles, who also ruled, or for Judah sharing his fate.

p: Zerubbabel led the first return from Babylon. Every name after him is found only here.
b: Shealtiel was Jeconiah's son (1 Chronicles 3:17). Ezra 3:2 and Haggai 1:1 call Zerubbabel "son of Shealtiel," though 1 Chronicles 3:19 makes him the son of Shealtiel's brother Pedaiah: perhaps by levirate marriage, or a different way of counting. Zerubbabel was governor of Judah and helped rebuild the Temple after 538 BC. The nine names that follow him, Abiud to Jacob, appear nowhere in the Old Testament. Matthew may have used family records like those Josephus says priestly families kept (Against Apion 1.30–36), or oral tradition. Luke's list runs through other names entirely (Luke 3:23–27).
r: 1 Chronicles 3:17–19; Ezra 3:2; Ezra 5:2; Haggai 1:1; Haggai 2:23; Luke 3:27

p: For 39 links a man "fathered" a son. Now Jesus "was born" from Mary, and Joseph fathers no one.
b: Matthew suddenly changes the verb: not "Joseph fathered Jesus" but "from her" (ex hēs, feminine) "was born" (passive) Jesus. The Greek makes clear that Jesus was born from Mary, and the passive leaves the true Father unnamed, a way Jewish writers often spoke of God's acts. Joseph is still named as "the husband of Mary," because through him Jesus belongs legally to David's line (see 1:25). Some early copies show scribes wrestling with this verse (see the variant).
orig: ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη Ἰησοῦς (ex hēs egennēthē Iēsous)

t: Two family trees: Matthew and Luke
p: Matthew says Joseph's father was Jacob; Luke says Heli. The two lists share almost no names from David to Joseph.
b: Luke 3:23–38 runs upward from Jesus to Adam and goes through David's son Nathan, not Solomon. Readers explain the difference in several ways. Levirate marriage: Julius Africanus (about AD 220, in Eusebius, Church History 1.7) said Jacob and Heli were half-brothers, and one raised up a son for the other who had died childless. Mary's line in Luke: from the late 1400s many have read Luke's list as Mary's family, with Heli as Joseph's father-in-law. Royal and natural lines: Matthew gives the legal heirs to the throne, Luke the physical descent. Two theological lists: many critical scholars think each writer built a list to make his own point (Matthew: the king of Israel; Luke: the son of Adam and of God), with little hope of reconciling them historically.

p: Fourteen is the number of David's name in Hebrew. The pattern shows history moving on God's schedule.
b: Matthew shapes the list into three eras: from Abraham to David (rise), from David to the exile (fall), from the exile to the Messiah (waiting). In Hebrew letters stand for numbers, and David's name, DWD, adds up to 4 + 6 + 4 = 14 (this use of letters is called gematria), so the whole list may spell out "David" three times. Others note that three fourteens make six sevens, so Jesus opens the seventh seven, the age of fulfillment, much as the "weeks" of Daniel 9:24–27 and 1 Enoch 93 divide history. The count is not exact: the last set has only thirteen names unless Jeconiah or Jesus is counted twice, and kings were left out to reach fourteen (see 1:8). Some manuscripts (Koridethi, family 1, 33 and others, as reported in the NA28 apparatus) even add "Josiah fathered Jehoiakim" in 1:11, which spoils the count. The point is pattern, not census.

p: A Jewish betrothal was a binding marriage contract. The couple lived together only after a later wedding.
b: Mnēsteuō stands for the Jewish betrothal (erusin or kiddushin). It was a legal marriage: the man is already called "her husband" (1:19), unfaithfulness counted as adultery (Deuteronomy 22:23–24), and only a divorce could end it. Usually about a year passed before the wedding, when the bride moved to her husband's home (Mishnah, Ketubot 5:2). Girls were often betrothed young, around twelve to fourteen. "Before they had come together" means before the wedding and before they lived together as husband and wife.

t: The virgin birth: how readers take it
p: Matthew and Luke tell it independently. Christians confess it in the creeds; historians debate it.
b: Matthew and Luke tell the story in very different ways, yet both say Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit before she lived with Joseph, so the belief is older than either Gospel. Traditional Christian view: a true miracle, confessed in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds, showing that Jesus is both truly human and from God. Critical views: many scholars say history cannot decide such a claim. Raymond Brown concluded that the evidence leaves it historically unresolved, though the tradition is early. Others read it as a theological story like the miraculous births of Isaac or Samson. The rumor of illegitimacy: by the 170s the pagan writer Celsus repeated a Jewish story that Jesus was the son of a soldier named Panthera (Origen, Against Celsus 1.28, 32). Some scholars think the charge goes back to Jesus' lifetime (compare John 8:41); Jane Schaberg argued that Matthew himself hints at it, a view most reject.
r: Luke 1:26–38; Luke 3:23; Mark 6:3; John 8:41; Galatians 4:4; Genesis 18:10–14; Judges 13:3

p: Was Joseph obeying the law, showing mercy, or stepping back in awe?
b: Dikaios, "righteous," usually means faithful to God's law. Law and mercy: most readers think that, as a law-keeping man, Joseph felt he could not marry a woman pregnant by someone else (compare Deuteronomy 22:20–24), but he chose the gentlest legal way, a quiet divorce before two witnesses, rather than a public trial. Matthew later makes mercy the heart of the law (9:13; 12:7). Mercy is the righteousness: some read "righteous" as "kind," so Joseph's kindness is his righteousness. Awe: a view found in some church fathers and medieval writers holds that Joseph already knew the child was from the Spirit and felt unworthy to take God's work as his own. Most commentators think the angel's words in 1:20 fit the first view best, though supporters of the third read "don't be afraid" in their favor.

p: Idou, "look," turns the hearer's eyes to something surprising. Matthew uses it over sixty times.
b: Idou translates the Hebrew hinneh, "look, here is." It marks a sudden appearance or a surprising turn, and it gives Matthew a biblical sound, since the Septuagint uses it constantly. The KJV renders it "behold." This translation keeps it as "look" in most places, so readers can see where Matthew wants them to pay attention.

t: Joseph the dreamer, son of Jacob
p: Like Joseph in Genesis, this Joseph, also a son of Jacob, receives God's guidance in dreams.
b: Matthew tells of five guiding dreams in the birth story (1:20; 2:12; 2:13; 2:19; 2:22), and four come to Joseph. The first readers would think of Joseph son of Jacob in Genesis, the "master dreamer" (Genesis 37:19), who also went down to Egypt and saved his family there. Matthew's Joseph is also a son of a Jacob (1:16), and he too takes the family to Egypt (2:13–15). "An angel of the Lord" recalls the messenger who spoke for God in the Old Testament stories (Genesis 16:7; Judges 13:3). Here, as there, the angel brings a promise of a son.

p: In Hebrew the wordplay is clear: Yeshua ("the LORD saves") will save (yoshia') his people.
b: The angel's reason, "for he is the one who will save," only makes sense if you know Hebrew or Aramaic: Yeshua sounds like yoshia', "he will save." Matthew expects his readers to know. The rescue is not first from Rome but "from their sins," which echoes Psalm 130:8, "And he is the one who will redeem Israel from all its guilty deeds," where God himself is the rescuer. "His people" means Israel first, but by the end of the Gospel it widens to all who follow him (28:19). The same theme returns at the Last Supper, where Jesus speaks of his blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins (26:28).

p: Ten times Matthew stops the story to say that an event fulfilled Scripture. This is the first.
b: Matthew's "formula quotations" are a mark of the book: 1:22–23; 2:15; 2:17–18; 2:23; 4:14–16; 8:17; 12:17–21; 13:35; 21:4–5; 27:9–10 (and 2:5–6 is close). Plēroō means "fill full." Sometimes it means a prediction came true. But often Matthew sees a pattern from Israel's story filled out in Jesus: Israel called out of Egypt (2:15), mothers weeping in exile (2:18). Jewish interpreters at Qumran read Scripture in a similar way, applying the prophets to their own day. Krister Stendahl argued that Matthew's quotations come from a "school" of Christian scribes who studied Scripture closely, and they often follow neither the Hebrew nor the Septuagint exactly.

p: Isaiah's Hebrew says 'almah, "young woman." The Greek Old Testament Matthew quotes says parthenos, "virgin."
b: In Isaiah 7:14 the Hebrew reads, "Look, the young woman is pregnant and about to have a son, and she will name him Immanuel." 'Almah means a young woman of marriageable age; it does not say whether she is a virgin. Traditional readers answer that none of its other uses (Genesis 24:43; Exodus 2:8; Psalm 68:25; Proverbs 30:19; Song of Songs 1:3; Song of Songs 6:8) clearly means a married woman, and Gordon Wenham has shown that even betulah, usually rendered "virgin," can mean simply a girl of marriageable age. The Septuagint, made by Jews before Jesus, chose parthenos, which usually means "virgin," though it once describes Dinah after she was raped (Genesis 34:3). In its first setting the sign was for King Ahaz in about 734 BC: before the child was old enough to choose, the two kings he feared would be gone (Isaiah 7:16). Jewish readers, from Trypho in Justin Martyr's Dialogue (about AD 155) to Rashi, read it of a child of that time. Christians read it as a direct prophecy, a sign with two fulfillments, or a pattern filled out in Jesus. Matthew also changes "she will name" to "they will give him the name."
r: Isaiah 7:10–17; Isaiah 8:3–4; Isaiah 8:8–10; Genesis 24:43; Genesis 34:3; Proverbs 30:19; Exodus 2:8; Psalm 68:25

p: Matthew opens with "God is with us" and ends with Jesus' promise to be with his followers always.
b: Immanuel is Hebrew for "with us is God" ('immanu El). In Isaiah it was a promise that God would stand by Judah (Isaiah 8:8, 10). Matthew explains the name for readers who did not know Hebrew, and he builds his whole Gospel around it. Halfway through, Jesus promises to be among two or three gathered in his name (18:20), and the Gospel's last words are his promise to be with his followers to the end of the age (28:20). The church fathers read the name as a statement of the incarnation: in Jesus, God himself is present with his people.

t: "Until": what it does and does not say
p: The verse says Joseph and Mary had no sex before the birth. Churches differ on what came after.
b: Heōs hou, "until," says what did not happen up to a point. By itself it does not say whether things changed afterward. Sometimes the context implies a change; sometimes it plainly does not, as in 2 Samuel 6:23, "Michal ... had no child until the day she died," and Jesus' promise to be with his followers until the end of the age (28:20), which does not stop then. The imperfect verb "was not knowing her" ("know" is the Bible's way of saying sex) stresses a lasting state. So the grammar leaves the question open. Matthew's own point is that no one could say Joseph was Jesus' natural father. Most Protestants read the verse, with the mention of Jesus' brothers (12:46; 13:55), as implying a normal marriage afterward. Catholic and Orthodox Christians held that Mary remained a virgin, and so did Luther, Zwingli and Wesley; Calvin declined to argue from this verse either way (see the chapter page).
orig: οὐκ ἐγίνωσκεν αὐτὴν ἕως οὗ (ouk eginōsken autēn heōs hou)

p: By naming the boy, Joseph claims him as his son, and so makes him a son of David.
b: In Jewish law a man's word that a child was his son settled the matter (Mishnah, Bava Batra 8:6: "This is my son"). By taking Mary home and naming the child, as the angel told him (1:21), Joseph acknowledges Jesus as his own heir. This is how Matthew can trace Jesus through Joseph's royal line and still say Joseph was not his natural father. The angel addressed Joseph as "son of David" (1:20) for this reason. Luke has Mary receive the name (Luke 1:31); Matthew gives the naming to Joseph.

p: A village five miles south of Jerusalem, home of Ruth, Boaz and David. Matthew says "of Judea" to mark the right one.
b: There was another Bethlehem in Galilee, in Zebulun's land (Joshua 19:15), so Matthew specifies the one in Judea, the hometown of David (1 Samuel 16:1; 17:12), where Ruth and Boaz lived and near which Rachel was buried (Genesis 35:19). Matthew does not mention the census of Luke 2:1–5 and seems to assume that Joseph's family already lived in Bethlehem; they move to Nazareth only later (2:23). Luke has them come from Nazareth and go back there. Both agree on the birth in Bethlehem. Justin Martyr (about AD 155) already speaks of the birth in a cave near the village, the site of today's Church of the Nativity.
r: Micah 5:2; 1 Samuel 16:1; 1 Samuel 17:12; Ruth 1:1–2; Genesis 35:19; Luke 2:1–7; John 7:42

t: Herod the Great and the date of Jesus' birth
p: Herod died in 4 BC by the usual reckoning, so Jesus was born a few years "before Christ."
b: Herod the Great ruled Judea for Rome from 37 BC until his death, which Josephus places after an eclipse of the moon and before a Passover, most likely in 4 BC (a few scholars argue for 1 BC). Our calendar comes from the monk Dionysius Exiguus (AD 525), who set Jesus' birth a few years too late. Since Herod killed boys "from two years old down" (2:16), Matthew points to a birth around 6–4 BC. Herod was an Idumean whose family had converted to Judaism, a brilliant builder (the Temple, Caesarea, Masada) and a suspicious, violent ruler.
l: Date of the birth of Jesus

p: Matthew never says there were three, never calls them kings, and never names them.
b: Magoi were first a priestly class of the Medes and Persians (Herodotus, Histories 1.101), experts in dreams and the stars. By Jesus' time the word covered astrologers, sages and also sorcerers (Acts 13:6, 8). The KJV calls them "wise men." "From the east" may mean Persia, Babylon (with its old Jewish community and its star-watchers) or Arabia, which Justin Martyr suggests because of the gifts. The number three comes from the three gifts (first in Origen). They became kings because readers joined them to Psalm 72:10–11 and Isaiah 60:3 (Tertullian already calls them "almost kings"). The names Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar appear in the West in the 500s. The church celebrates them at Epiphany (January 6).

p: A miracle, a planetary conjunction, a comet, or a sign read by astrologers? Readers have proposed all of these.
b: En tē anatolē can mean "in the east" (KJV) or "at its rising," an astronomers' term. A miracle: a star that goes ahead and stops over one house (2:9) does not act like any natural star; Ignatius of Antioch (about AD 110) describes it as outshining all the others. A conjunction: Johannes Kepler (1606) pointed to the meeting of Jupiter and Saturn in Pisces in 7 BC. A comet or nova: Chinese records note a new "broom star" in 5 BC, which Colin Humphreys argues was the star. An astrological sign: Michael Molnar argues that the moon passed in front of Jupiter, the royal planet, in Aries, the sign linked to Judea, in 6 BC. Many readers also hear Balaam's prophecy, "A star will march out of Jacob" (Numbers 24:17), which Jews applied to the Messiah.
orig: τὸν ἀστέρα ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ (ton astera en tē anatolē)

t: "King of the Jews": first and last
p: Gentiles call Jesus "king of the Jews" at his birth, and Gentiles will call him that again at his death.
b: In Matthew the title is used only by Gentiles: the magi here, then Pilate, the soldiers and the charge nailed above the cross (27:11, 29, 37). Jews in Matthew say "king of Israel" (27:42). The magi's question would sound like treason to Herod, whom the Roman Senate had named king of Judea, and who was not of David's line. The scene sets up the Gospel's pattern: outsiders see, the rulers in Jerusalem are alarmed.

p: Proskyneō means to kneel or bow low. It can be honor given to a king or worship given to God.
b: Proskyneō describes falling to the ground before someone greater: a king, a master, or God. The magi come to honor a newborn king, and Herod pretends he wants to do the same (2:8). But Matthew uses the word thirteen times, ten of them for people kneeling before Jesus (2:2, 8, 11; 8:2; 9:18; 14:33; 15:25; 20:20; 28:9, 17), and in 4:9–10 Jesus says it belongs only to God. So Matthew's readers would hear more than court manners: the nations kneel before one who is "God with us" (1:23). Translations choose "worship" (KJV, most modern) or "pay homage." This translation says "bow down to" in every one of these scenes, keeping the bodily act and leaving the reader to see who deserves it.

a: the whole city of Jerusalem along with him
p: The city that should welcome its king is alarmed. Matthew uses the same picture when Jesus enters at the end.
b: Etarachthē means stirred up, thrown into turmoil. Herod's alarm is understandable: he killed even his own sons when he suspected them of plotting. Why "the whole city"? Perhaps people feared what Herod would do, or what a new king might bring. Matthew repeats the picture when Jesus rides into Jerusalem: "the entire city was shaken" (21:10, with a stronger verb). From the beginning, the capital is where Jesus meets opposition.

p: The Temple's priestly leaders and the experts in the law of Moses. They know the answer but do not go.
b: "Chief priests" means the high priest, former high priests and the leading priestly families who ran the Temple. "Scribes" (grammateis) were trained experts in the law of Moses, who copied, taught and applied it; many were Pharisees, some were priests. Together they appear later as the people who hand Jesus over (16:21; 20:18). Here they give the right answer from Scripture at once, yet no one travels the five miles to Bethlehem. The foreigners who read the stars seek the king; the experts in the Scriptures stay home. Matthew notes the contrast without comment.

a: And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah
p: Matthew joins two texts and changes Micah's "small" to "in no way the least."
b: Micah 5:2 (5:1 in Hebrew) reads: "But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, too small to be among the clans of Judah, from you one will come out for me to be ruler in Israel." Matthew's form differs in three ways. He says Bethlehem is "in no way the least," turning Micah's point around: the small town has become great because of the child born there. He has "leaders" where Micah has "clans"; the Hebrew letters can be read either way ('alfe, "clans, thousands," or 'allufe, "chiefs"). And he ends with words God spoke to David, "You are the one who will shepherd my people Israel" (2 Samuel 5:2). Jewish tradition too read Micah 5:2 of the Messiah (the Targum on Micah). John 7:42 shows that this was well known.

p: By the time the magi come, the family is living in a house, and the child may be up to two years old.
b: Matthew says nothing of a manger or shepherds; those come from Luke 2:7–20. The magi find "the child" (paidion, a young child, not a newborn) in "the house," and Herod's order to kill boys up to two years old (2:16) suggests some months had passed since the star appeared. Christmas scenes that put the magi beside the manger blend two Gospels and two moments. Readers who see Matthew and Luke as independent accounts point out that they agree on the main facts (Bethlehem, Mary, Joseph, Herod, Nazareth) while telling different episodes.

p: Gifts fit for a king. The church fathers read them as gifts for a king, for God and for one who would die.
b: Gold, frankincense (a fragrant resin burned as incense in the Temple) and myrrh (a perfumed resin used in oils and in burial) were costly goods of the spice routes of Arabia. Isaiah 60:6 pictures nations coming with "gold and frankincense," and Psalm 72:10–15 has kings bringing gifts and "Sheba's gold" to the king. From Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.9.2) on, Christians read the gifts as gold for a king, incense for God and myrrh for a man who would die and be buried. Myrrh reappears at the cross and the tomb (Mark 15:23; John 19:39).
r: Isaiah 60:6; Psalm 72:10; Psalm 72:15; Song of Songs 3:6; Exodus 30:23–24; Exodus 30:34; Mark 15:23; John 19:39

p: A king kills boys, a child escapes, and the family returns when "the ones who wanted the child's life have died."
b: Matthew's readers would hear the story of Moses. Pharaoh ordered every newborn Hebrew boy thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1:22); Moses ran from Pharaoh, who wanted to kill him (Exodus 2:15); and God told him to go back, because "The men who wanted your life have all died" (Exodus 4:19). Matthew 2:20 uses almost the same words. Jewish retellings in Jesus' day added that Pharaoh learned of the coming deliverer from his scribes or from a dream (Josephus, Antiquities 2.205–209), as Herod learns from his scribes here. Egypt was also a common place of refuge for Jews; Alexandria had a huge Jewish community. Matthew goes on to present Jesus as the new Moses, especially on the mountain in 5:1.
r: Exodus 1:15–22; Exodus 2:15; Exodus 4:19–20; Genesis 46:3–4; 1 Kings 11:40; Jeremiah 26:21; 2:20; 5:1

a: Out of Egypt I called my son
p: In Hosea "my son" is the nation of Israel coming out of Egypt. Matthew sees Jesus living out Israel's story.
b: Hosea 11:1 reads, "When Israel was a boy, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son." It looks back to the exodus, as in Exodus 4:22, "Israel is my son, my firstborn." Hosea was not predicting the Messiah, and Matthew surely knew that. His point is a pattern: Jesus, God's Son, repeats in his own life the story of God's son Israel: down to Egypt, out of Egypt, through the waters (3:13–17), tested in the wilderness (4:1–11). Matthew's words follow the Hebrew; the Septuagint has "I called his children." He places the quotation at the flight into Egypt, looking ahead to the return.
orig: Ἐξ Αἰγύπτου ἐκάλεσα τὸν υἱόν μου (Ex Aigyptou ekalesa ton huion mou)

a: He sent men to kill every boy in Bethlehem
p: No other ancient source mentions this killing. Historians weigh it in light of Herod's known cruelty.
b: Josephus describes Herod's brutality in detail: he killed his wife Mariamne, three of his sons and many nobles, and near death ordered leading men to be executed so that there would be mourning when he died (Antiquities 17.174–181). He does not mention Bethlehem. Bethlehem was small, perhaps a few hundred people, so the boys killed may have numbered ten or twenty, which might not have reached the records. Many historians therefore think the event is possible but cannot be confirmed; others see it as a story built on Pharaoh and Moses. A Latin writer of the 400s, Macrobius, reports Augustus's joke that it was better to be Herod's pig than his son, in a passage that mentions boys under two killed by Herod in Syria (Saturnalia 2.4.11), but it is late and may depend on Christian sources. The church remembers these children as the Holy Innocents (December 28, or December 29 in the East).

a: Then the word spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled
p: Here Matthew does not say "so that" as in 1:22 and 2:15. God did not plan the children's death.
b: Most of Matthew's fulfillment formulas use hina or hopōs, "so that" (1:22; 2:15; 2:23). Twice the formula begins instead with tote, "then": here, at the killing of the children, and at Judas's death (27:9). Many interpreters, from the church fathers on, see a deliberate choice: Matthew will not say that God intended an evil act, only that Scripture had already given words to such grief.

a: Rachel is weeping for her children
p: Jeremiah pictures Rachel, mother of the tribes, weeping as her children go into exile. Hope follows at once.
b: Rachel, Jacob's beloved wife, died giving birth to Benjamin and was buried "on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem" (Genesis 35:19), though 1 Samuel 10:2 puts her grave in Benjamin's land, near Ramah, north of Jerusalem. In Jeremiah 31:15 she weeps from her grave as the people are led away; Ramah was where the Babylonians gathered the captives (Jeremiah 40:1). Matthew applies the scene to Bethlehem's mothers. The next verses in Jeremiah promise, "the children will come home to their own borders" (Jeremiah 31:16–17), and Jeremiah 31:31–34 promises a new covenant, which Matthew's readers would know Jesus spoke of at his last supper (26:28).

a: Archelaus now ruled Judea in place of his father Herod
t: Archelaus, the worst of Herod's sons
p: Archelaus ruled Judea from 4 BC to AD 6 so brutally that Rome removed him.
b: At Herod's death his kingdom was split among three sons. Archelaus got Judea, Samaria and Idumea with the title ethnarch ("ruler of a people"), not king, though people called him king. He began by having about three thousand people killed in the Temple courts at Passover (Josephus, Antiquities 17.213–218). After nine years of complaints Augustus banished him to Gaul in AD 6 and put Judea under a Roman governor; that is how Pilate came to rule there. Galilee went to his brother Herod Antipas, a safer place for Joseph's family. Some think Jesus' parable of the nobleman who went abroad to receive a kingdom, and whom his people did not want (Luke 19:12–14), recalls Archelaus's trip to Rome.

a: He will be called a Nazarene
p: No verse in the Old Testament says this. Matthew writes "the prophets," plural, and leaves readers to work it out.
b: Readers have made several suggestions, and they can be combined. The Branch: Isaiah 11:1 calls the coming king a netser, "shoot" or "branch," from Jesse's roots, and Nazareth may come from the same root (Jerome and many since). Other prophets call him "the Branch" with a different word (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8). The Nazirite: Samson was to be "God's Nazirite from the womb" (Judges 13:5), and the Septuagint has a similar-sounding word, though Jesus was no Nazirite (11:19). The despised one: Nazareth was an obscure village ("Something good, out of Nazareth? Is that possible?" John 1:46), so the title recalls prophecies of a rejected Messiah (Isaiah 53:3; Psalm 22:6). Matthew's Greek is Nazōraios, the name later given to Jesus' followers (Acts 24:5); Hebrew still calls Christians Notsrim.
r: Isaiah 11:1; Isaiah 53:3; Judges 13:5; Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 6:12; John 1:46; Acts 24:5; 26:71

p: A prophet who drew crowds to the Jordan around AD 28. Josephus describes him too.
b: Matthew introduces John without background; Luke 1 makes him the son of the priest Zechariah and a relative of Jesus. Josephus, writing about AD 94, calls him "a good man" who urged Jews to live justly and devoutly and "to come together by baptism," and says Herod Antipas executed him for fear his influence might lead to a revolt (Antiquities 18.116–119; see 14:1–12). John's title, ho baptistēs, means "the one who immerses": his practice was unusual enough to become his name. Some scholars think he had contact with the community at Qumran, which also lived in the Judean wilderness and read Isaiah 40:3 of itself, but this is unproven.

p: Israel became God's people in the wilderness, and the prophets promised a new beginning there.
b: The Judean wilderness is the dry, empty land that falls from the hills east of Jerusalem down to the Dead Sea and the Jordan valley. For Israel the wilderness meant the forty years after the exodus, when God led and tested his people (Deuteronomy 8:2). The prophets promised a new exodus that would start there (Isaiah 40:3; Hosea 2:14). In Jesus' century several would-be prophets led crowds into the wilderness, expecting God to act (Josephus, Antiquities 20.97–98, 167–168). John's choice of place was itself a message: the new exodus is beginning. Jesus too will be tested in the wilderness (4:1).

p: Metanoeō means a change of mind and direction. The Latin "do penance" started a famous argument.
b: Metanoeō is literally "change your mind," but in the Bible it carries the weight of the Hebrew shuv, "turn back" (to God): a change of life, not only of feelings. The Latin Vulgate rendered it paenitentiam agite, which medieval readers often took as "do penance," the church's practice of confession and works of satisfaction. Erasmus's Greek New Testament (1516) argued that the word meant "come to your senses." Luther's first of the Ninety-Five Theses (1517) begins from this word: "When our Lord and Master Jesus Christ said 'Repent' (4:17), he willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance." John and Jesus begin with the same call (4:17).

p: Matthew's usual phrase. "Heaven" is a respectful Jewish way of saying "God"; the kingdom is God's rule.
b: Matthew writes "kingdom of heaven" about 32 times where Mark and Luke say "kingdom of God." Jews often avoided saying "God" out of reverence and said "Heaven" instead (as the prodigal son says, "I have sinned against heaven," Luke 15:18). So the phrase does not mean a place in the sky. Basileia means kingship or reign: God ruling as king, as the prophets promised (Daniel 2:44; Isaiah 52:7). "Has drawn near" (ēngiken, perfect tense) is debated: "is close at hand" (soon), or "has arrived" (already here in Jesus, compare 12:28). Many readers hold both: the kingdom is already breaking in and not yet complete.
orig: ἤγγικεν ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν (ēngiken hē basileia tōn ouranōn)

a: A voice is shouting in the wilderness
t: Isaiah 40:3: the voice and the road
p: In Isaiah the road is made for God's return from exile. Matthew applies "the Lord" to Jesus.
b: Isaiah 40 opens the prophet's message of comfort to exiles in Babylon: God himself is coming home with his people, and a road must be built through the desert. The Hebrew reads, "A voice calls out: In the wilderness clear the way of the LORD!" The Greek Old Testament, which Matthew follows, puts the voice itself in the wilderness, which fits John. The community at Qumran used the same verse to explain why they had gone out into the wilderness to study the law (Community Rule 1QS 8:13–16). Where Isaiah has the divine name, Matthew's "the Lord" now points to Jesus, whose way John prepares, and he changes Isaiah's "paths of our God" to "paths for him."

a: a garment of camel hair and a leather belt tied around his waist
p: John's clothes copy Elijah's. Malachi promised that Elijah would come back before the day of the Lord.
b: When King Ahaziah's messengers described the prophet they had met, "He was a hairy man," they said, "with a leather loincloth tied around his waist," and the king knew: "That was Elijah the Tishbite" (2 Kings 1:8). A rough hair cloak was the prophet's mark (Zechariah 13:4). Malachi 4:5 promised that God would send Elijah before the great day of the LORD, and Jews expected his return. Matthew's readers are meant to recognize Elijah in John's clothes; Jesus says so outright later (11:14; 17:12–13). In John 1:21 John himself denies being Elijah, probably meaning he was not Elijah come back in person.
r: 2 Kings 1:8; Zechariah 13:4; Malachi 3:1; Malachi 4:5–6; 11:14; 17:10–13; John 1:21; Luke 1:17

p: Locusts were clean food under the law. Wild honey was from wild bees or from date and tree sap.
b: Leviticus 11:22 allows four kinds of locusts as food, and the poor and desert peoples ate them dried or roasted. The Damascus Document from Qumran even gives rules for cooking them (CD 12:14–15). "Wild honey" was either honey from wild bees in rocks (Deuteronomy 32:13; Judges 14:8) or the sweet sap of trees. The point is that John lived on what the wilderness gave, depending on God like Israel and Elijah in the desert. Later some groups made him a vegetarian: the Gospel of the Ebionites, quoted by Epiphanius in the 300s, changed "locusts" into "cakes."

a: he baptized them in the Jordan River
p: Jews washed often for purity. John's baptism was different: once, at his hands, for repentance.
b: Baptizō means to dip or immerse. Jews in Jesus' time washed themselves in stepped immersion pools (miqva'ot), many of which archaeologists have found near the Temple and in homes, to be clean for worship. The Qumran community washed daily. Later rabbinic law also required Gentile converts to immerse themselves, though it is debated whether this was done before AD 70. John's baptism differed: it was given once, by John himself, in a flowing river, to people already Jewish, and it was tied to confessing sins and to the coming judgment. Mark 1:4 calls it "a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins." Josephus says it purified the body after the soul had been cleansed by right living.
r: Mark 1:4–5; Luke 3:3; John 3:23; Acts 19:3–5; Leviticus 15:13; Ezekiel 36:25

t: Who were the Pharisees and Sadducees?
p: Two Jewish parties that usually disagreed. Matthew often pairs them as opponents of Jesus.
b: The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to keeping the law with care in daily life, including purity, tithing and the Sabbath, and to the "traditions of the elders" that applied it. They believed in the resurrection and in angels, and they were respected by many ordinary people (Josephus, Antiquities 18.12–15). The Sadducees were a smaller group tied to the high-priestly families; they accepted only the written law and denied the resurrection (22:23; Acts 23:8). The two parties were rivals, so John's address to both is surprising; Matthew often groups them (16:1–12) as the leaders of the people. After AD 70 the Sadducees vanished, and the Pharisees' heirs, the rabbis, shaped Judaism. Matthew's sharp words against them belong to his own community's dispute with those heirs, and most historians now agree (E. P. Sanders, Anthony Saldarini) that they should not be read as a fair picture of Pharisees in general. Luke 3:7 addresses the same words to "the crowds."

p: John pictures snakes racing out of a burning field: they run from danger without changing.
b: Gennēmata echidnōn, "offspring of vipers," was a harsh insult: children of a deadly, deceiving creature (compare Isaiah 59:5 and the serpent of Genesis 3). When farmers burned a field after harvest, snakes fled in front of the flames. John's image says these leaders came out of fear of judgment, not true repentance. Jesus uses the same words twice in Matthew (12:34; 23:33). The "coming anger" is God's judgment at the end, which the prophets called the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:1; Zephaniah 1:14–18).

a: God can raise up children for Abraham from these very stones
p: In Hebrew and Aramaic "stones" and "sons" sound alike: avanim and banim.
b: John's saying likely carried a wordplay: Hebrew avanim (stones) and banim (sons); Aramaic avnaya and benaya. Isaiah had told Israel to "look at the rock that you were hewn out of ... Look at Abraham, your ancestor" (Isaiah 51:1–2). John warns that descent from Abraham is no shelter from judgment: God can make new children for Abraham out of the river stones. Jewish teachers also stressed that Abraham's true children act like him (compare Mishnah Avot 5:19 on the disciples of Abraham), and Paul and John's Gospel make a similar point (Romans 4:16; John 8:39). The saying prepares for Gentiles being counted among Abraham's family (8:11).
orig: ἐκ τῶν λίθων τούτων ἐγεῖραι τέκνα τῷ Ἀβραάμ
r: Isaiah 51:1–2; 8:11; Luke 3:8; John 8:33–39; Romans 4:16; Romans 9:7–8; Galatians 3:7

a: The ax already lies against the root of the trees
t: The ax and the fruitless tree
p: Judgment is not far off; the woodcutter has already set his ax to the trunk.
b: Isaiah pictured God cutting down proud forests with an ax (Isaiah 10:33–34). John's tree is a person or a people, and the fruit is a changed life (3:8). The present tense, "is being cut down," makes the judgment sound already under way. The same Greek line returns in the Sermon on the Mount (7:19), and the theme of fruit runs through Matthew (12:33; 21:19, 43).

a: I am not good enough even to carry his sandals
p: Carrying or untying a master's sandals was work for the lowest slave.
b: A later rabbinic saying holds that a disciple should do for his teacher everything a slave does for his master, except take off his sandals, which was too degrading (Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 96a). John ranks himself lower than a slave next to the one who is coming. Mark 1:7, Luke 3:16 and John 1:27 have "untie the strap of his sandals"; Matthew has "carry." The "stronger one" is God's agent of the end; Matthew's readers know it is Jesus.

t: Baptized in the Spirit and fire
p: Is the fire judgment, purification, or the flames of Pentecost?
b: John's water baptism points to a greater baptism. Judgment: in 3:10 and 3:12 fire burns the fruitless tree and the chaff, so the coming one brings the Spirit to the repentant and fire to the rest. Purification: one baptism that cleanses, as metal is refined (Malachi 3:2–3; Isaiah 4:4); the prophets promised God would pour out his Spirit and wash his people (Ezekiel 36:25–27; Joel 2:28). Pentecost: many Christian readers see its fulfillment in the tongues of fire and the Spirit given in Acts 2:3–4. Pentecostal churches read it as a baptism in the Spirit that can follow conversion. Many scholars think John meant judgment and cleansing together, and that Christians later heard more in it. The Byzantine text lacks "and fire" (see the variant).
r: 3:10; 3:12; Malachi 3:2–3; Isaiah 4:4; Ezekiel 36:25–27; Joel 2:28–29; Acts 1:5; Acts 2:1–4; Acts 11:16

a: He holds his winnowing fork in his hand
p: Farmers tossed threshed grain into the wind: the heavy wheat fell, the light chaff blew away.
b: After harvest, grain was spread on a flat, hard threshing floor and crushed by animals or sledges. Then the farmer used a wooden fork to throw it into the evening breeze. The wheat fell back; the chaff, the husks, blew aside and was swept up and burned. The prophets used the picture for judgment (Psalm 1:4; Isaiah 41:15–16; Jeremiah 15:7). "His" threshing floor means the one coming owns the harvest: he is the judge. The "fire no one can put out" is a phrase from Isaiah 66:24, used again in Mark 9:43–48.

a: He came to John to be baptized by him
t: A fact the church found hard
p: Historians count Jesus' baptism by John among the surest facts of his life, because it embarrassed his followers.
b: All four Gospels connect Jesus with John's baptism (Mark 1:9–11; Luke 3:21–22; John 1:29–34). Historians see it as almost certainly true for a simple reason: the early church would hardly invent a story in which Jesus submits to a baptism "for repentance" from someone else, as if he were John's follower or had sins to confess. The Gospels show signs of that discomfort: Matthew adds John's protest (3:14–15), Luke tells of the baptism only after John is in prison (Luke 3:20–21), and John's Gospel does not describe it at all. Jesus came from Galilee, about 60 to 70 miles (100 km) north.

p: Only Matthew has John protest. It answers the question readers were asking: why would Jesus need baptism?
b: In Mark 1:9 Jesus is simply baptized. Matthew adds a dialogue (3:14–15) that admits the problem and answers it. Other early Christians felt the same difficulty. In a Jewish-Christian gospel that Jerome calls "according to the Hebrews" (Against the Pelagians 3.2), usually classed today as the Gospel of the Nazarenes, Jesus' mother and brothers urge him to go to John's baptism, and he answers, "What sin have I committed, that I should go and be baptized by him?" The imperfect verb, "was trying to stop," shows John holding back for some time.

p: Jesus' first words in Matthew. What do they mean?
b: These are Jesus' first words in the Gospel. "Righteousness" (dikaiosynē) in Matthew usually means doing what God requires (5:6, 10, 20; 6:1, 33). Readers explain the phrase in several ways. Obedience: God sent John (21:32), so it is right to accept his baptism; Jesus does everything God asks. Solidarity: he stands with the sinful people he came to save, like the Servant who "was counted with the rebels" and makes many righteous (Isaiah 53:11–12). Fulfilling Scripture: "fulfill" is Matthew's word for prophecy (1:22) and for the law (5:17), so Jesus completes God's saving plan. The church fathers added that he made the waters holy for Christian baptism (Ignatius, To the Ephesians 18:2). Ignatius also echoes this verse in To the Smyrnaeans 1:1.

a: God's Spirit coming down like a dove
p: The Spirit anoints Jesus for his work. The dove recalls creation and the flood.
b: The prophets promised that God's Spirit would rest on the coming king and servant (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1). Here that anointing happens: Jesus is the Messiah, the "anointed one." Why a dove? Readers hear creation, where "God's Spirit fluttered over the face of the waters" (Genesis 1:2); a later rabbinic comment compares that hovering to a dove's (Babylonian Talmud, Hagigah 15a). They also hear the flood, when the dove brought Noah news of a new world (Genesis 8:8–12), so the baptism marks a new creation. The "opened" heavens recall Isaiah 64:1 and Ezekiel 1:1, where heaven opens for God to act or to give a vision.
r: Isaiah 11:2; Isaiah 42:1; Isaiah 61:1; Isaiah 64:1; Genesis 1:2; Genesis 8:8–12; Ezekiel 1:1; John 1:32–34; Acts 10:38

a: This is my dearly loved Son; in him I take delight
p: The words blend Psalm 2 (the king), Isaiah 42 (the servant) and perhaps Genesis 22 (Isaac, the beloved son).
b: "My Son" recalls God's words to the king in Psalm 2:7, "You are my son." "In him I take delight" recalls Isaiah 42:1, the servant on whom God puts his Spirit; Matthew quotes that passage in full in 12:18. "Dearly loved" (agapētos, beloved) is the word the Septuagint uses for Isaac, "your son, ... your only one, whom you love" (Genesis 22:2). So the voice names Jesus as king, servant and beloved son at once. In Mark 1:11 and Luke 3:22 the voice speaks to Jesus ("You are"); in Matthew it announces him to others ("This is"), as at the transfiguration (17:5). From early times Christians saw the Trinity here: the Son in the water, the Spirit descending, the Father speaking.
r: Psalm 2:7; Isaiah 42:1; Genesis 22:2; Genesis 22:12; 12:18; 17:5; Mark 1:11; Luke 3:22; 2 Peter 1:17

p: Peirazō means both. God tests to prove; the devil tempts to break. Both are at work here.
b: Peirazō can mean to test, to try out, or to tempt to do wrong. English must choose; the Greek holds both. The Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness, as God "led" Israel there forty years "to humble you and to test you, to know what was in your heart" (Deuteronomy 8:2). The devil, "the tester" (4:3), uses the same moment to try to pull him away from God. The KJV and most English Bibles say "tempted"; this translation says "test," because the story is about proving what kind of Son Jesus is. The same word returns in the Lord's Prayer (6:13).

p: Moses fasted forty days and nights on the mountain; Elijah walked forty days; Israel wandered forty years.
b: Moses "was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights. Bread he did not eat, and water he did not drink" (Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 9:9). Elijah went "forty days and forty nights, all the way to God's mountain, Horeb" (1 Kings 19:8). Israel spent forty years in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 8:2). Only Matthew adds "and forty nights" (compare Mark 1:13; Luke 4:2), which makes the link to Moses exact. A fast of this length is near the limit of human survival; the point is that Jesus is utterly dependent on God.
r: Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 9:9; Deuteronomy 9:18; 1 Kings 19:8; Deuteronomy 8:2; Numbers 14:34; Mark 1:13; Luke 4:2

p: The devil does not doubt it. He takes the voice of 3:17 and tries to turn it into a reason to disobey.
b: The Greek "if" (ei with the indicative) assumes the statement is true: "Since you are God's Son." The voice at the baptism has just said, "This is my Son" (3:17). The tests are about what kind of Son Jesus will be: one who uses his power for himself, forces God's hand, or grabs the world's power, or one who trusts and obeys like a true son. The same taunt returns at the cross (27:40). Israel too was God's son (2:15; Exodus 4:22) and failed its tests in the wilderness.
orig: Εἰ υἱὸς εἶ τοῦ θεοῦ (Ei huios ei tou theou)

a: People will not live by bread alone
p: Each answer comes from Deuteronomy 6–8, Moses' words about Israel's forty years. Jesus passes the tests Israel failed.
b: Deuteronomy 8:3 says God let Israel go hungry and fed them manna "to teach you that people do not live by bread alone. People live by everything that comes out of the LORD's mouth." Jesus' other answers come from Deuteronomy 6:16 (4:7) and 6:13 (4:10). In the wilderness Israel complained about food, tested God at Massah and made a golden calf. Jesus, hungry, trusts God's word; refuses to test God; and worships God alone. Birger Gerhardsson argued that the three tests follow the Shema, "Love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your being and with all your strength" (Deuteronomy 6:5), as later Jewish teachers explained it: the heart (desire), the life (risked at the Temple) and the strength (wealth and power).
r: Deuteronomy 8:2–5; Deuteronomy 6:4–5; Deuteronomy 6:13; Deuteronomy 6:16; Exodus 16:2–4; John 4:34; John 6:31–35

a: the high corner of the Temple
p: Pterygion, "little wing," probably meant a high corner of the Temple walls above the Kidron Valley.
b: The word is unclear: the corner of the roof of a Temple building, the top of a gate, or most likely the southeast corner of Herod's great platform. There the Royal Porch stood high above the Kidron Valley; Josephus says anyone looking down from it would grow dizzy (Antiquities 15.411–412). A later Christian story says James, the Lord's brother, was thrown down from the "wing of the Temple" (Hegesippus, in Eusebius, Church History 2.23). "The holy city" is Jerusalem, as in Isaiah 52:1 and 27:53.
orig: τὸ πτερύγιον τοῦ ἱεροῦ (to pterygion tou hierou)

p: The tester answers with Scripture too, Psalm 91:11–12, but uses a promise of trust as a dare.
b: Psalm 91 promises God's care to the one who shelters in him: "For he will give his angels orders about you, to guard you on every road you take. Their hands will hold you up, so your foot does not hit a stone" (Psalm 91:11–12). The devil leaves out "to guard you on every road you take" and turns a promise for the dangers of ordinary life into a stunt to force God to act. Jesus does not argue about the psalm; he answers with another Scripture that shows how to read it. Ancient readers noted that knowing Bible verses is not the same as obeying God.

a: You must not put the Lord your God to the test
p: At Massah, Israel demanded a sign: "Is the LORD here with us, or isn't he?" Jesus refuses to make that demand.
b: Deuteronomy 6:16 says, "Do not put the LORD your God to the test, the way you tested him at Massah." At Massah the thirsty Israelites "put the LORD on trial, saying, 'Is the LORD here with us, or isn't he?'" (Exodus 17:7). To jump from the Temple and dare God to catch him would be the same demand for proof. Matthew's readers would notice the irony: the child named "God is with us" (1:23) does not need to test whether God is with him. As the Greek has no divine name, the Plain English Translation says "the Lord" where Deuteronomy has the LORD (see the note on 1:23 and terms).

p: Moses saw the whole promised land from Mount Nebo. The devil shows Jesus every kingdom on earth.
b: Before he died, Moses climbed Mount Nebo and "the LORD let him see the whole land" (Deuteronomy 34:1–4). The devil offers more: all the world's kingdoms, if Jesus will worship him. Mountains matter in Matthew: the Sermon on the Mount (5:1), the feeding (15:29), the transfiguration (17:1), the Mount of Olives (24:3), and the last mountain in Galilee where the risen Jesus says all authority has been given to him (28:16–18). There he receives from the Father, by the way of the cross, what the devil offered here without it. No mountain can show the whole world; the vision is beyond nature, which some read as a visionary experience.

p: Satan is Hebrew for "adversary"; "devil" is Greek diabolos, "slanderer." Jesus will use the same rebuke to Peter.
b: Satanas comes from Hebrew satan, "adversary, accuser," the title of the accuser in Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3. Diabolos (4:1, 5, 8, 11) is the Greek translation, "slanderer." Jesus' command hypage, "go away," returns in 16:23, when Peter tries to steer him away from the cross: "Get behind me, Satan." Both are the same test, to gain the kingdom without suffering. Many manuscripts add "behind me" here too (see the variant).

a: It is the Lord your God you must bow down to, and him alone you must serve
p: Deuteronomy 6:13 says "fear"; Matthew's Greek says "bow down to," answering the devil's demand.
b: Deuteronomy 6:13 reads, "It is the LORD your God you must fear. He is the one you must serve." Matthew's form has "bow down to" (proskyneō), as some Septuagint manuscripts do, and adds "alone," which sharpens the answer to the devil's "bow down to me" (4:9). The verse comes just after the Shema, "The LORD is our God. The LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Jesus refuses to share worship with anyone but God, yet in Matthew people bow down to Jesus himself (2:11; 14:33; 28:9, 17), which the church read as a sign of who he is.

a: angels came and took care of him
p: Like Elijah in the wilderness, Jesus is cared for by angels, without demanding it.
b: In 1 Kings 19:5–8 an angel woke Elijah and gave him food for his forty-day journey. Here angels come to Jesus after the tests. The verb diakoneō, "serve, wait on," often means serving food, so his hunger (4:2) is likely meant. Jesus refused to make angels catch him on the devil's terms (4:6); now God sends them in his own time. Mark 1:13 adds that he was with the wild animals.

p: The word used for John's arrest is the word Matthew will use for Jesus, betrayed and given up to death.
b: Paredothē means "was handed over." Most English Bibles say John "had been put in prison" (see 14:3), which is the meaning, but they lose the link Matthew draws: Jesus will be "handed over" to the authorities (17:22; 20:18–19; 26:2), and the disciples will be handed over too (10:17–21; 24:9). What happens to the forerunner will happen to the Messiah and to his followers. "Withdrew" is Matthew's word for moving away from danger (2:12–14; 2:22; 12:15; 14:13).

p: A fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee. A house there was honored as Peter's from early times.
b: Capernaum (Hebrew Kfar Nahum, "Nahum's village") lay on the lake's north shore near the border between Antipas's Galilee and Philip's territory, with a customs post (9:9). Matthew calls it Jesus' "own town" (9:1). Excavations have found basalt houses, a white limestone synagogue from the 300s or 400s built on older basalt foundations, and a house that was turned into a place of Christian meeting in the first centuries and later covered by an eight-sided church: pilgrims honored it as Peter's house (8:14). Jesus later pronounces judgment on the town for not repenting (11:23).

p: Zebulun and Naphtali were the first to fall to Assyria. Isaiah promised they would be the first to see the light.
b: In 733 BC the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser took "Galilee, all the land of Naphtali" and "carried the people off into exile" (2 Kings 15:29). Isaiah 9:1–2 (8:23–9:1 in Hebrew) promised that the land first humbled would be honored: "The people walking in the dark have seen a great light" (Isaiah 9:2). The next verses speak of a child born to be king on David's throne (Isaiah 9:6–7). Isaiah's "Galilee of the nations" reflected foreign settlement after the conquest. In Jesus' day, Galilee was mostly Jewish (archaeologists find Jewish stone vessels and immersion pools in its villages), but it was ringed by Gentile cities. Matthew sees the phrase as a hint of the mission to all nations (28:19).

a: From then on Jesus began to preach
t: A turning point in the book's structure
p: "From then on Jesus began" appears here and at 16:21. Some read it as the Gospel's main division.
b: How is Matthew built? Five books: B. W. Bacon (1930) saw five blocks of teaching, each closing "when Jesus had finished" (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1), like the five books of Moses, with chapters 1–4 as prologue. Three parts: Jack Dean Kingsbury pointed to "From then on Jesus began" here and in 16:21, which divides the book into the person of Jesus (1:1–4:16), his preaching (4:17–16:20) and his suffering and rising (16:21–28:20). Many scholars combine the two. Jesus' first message repeats John's word for word (3:2): see the notes there on "Repent" and "the kingdom of heaven."

p: Simon is always named first among the Twelve. "Peter" means "rock"; Matthew explains the name in 16:18.
b: Simon (Hebrew Shimon) and his brother Andrew came from Bethsaida (John 1:44) and lived in Capernaum (8:14). "Peter" is the Greek Petros, "rock," for the Aramaic Kepha (Cephas); Matthew uses the nickname from the start and tells its meaning later (16:18). Fishing on the lake was a solid trade, done in family partnerships, and taxed by the authorities. The brothers cast a round net by hand from the shore or the shallows. In John 1:35–42 Andrew had first been a disciple of John the Baptist, which may explain their quick response here.

p: Jewish students usually chose their teacher. Jesus calls his disciples himself, as Elijah called Elisha.
b: Later Jewish teaching advised, "Make for yourself a teacher" (Mishnah Avot 1:6): students sought out a rabbi. Jesus does the choosing, and he calls them to follow him, not to study the law with him. The closest model is a prophet: Elijah found Elisha plowing and threw his cloak over him, and Elisha "left the oxen and ran after Elijah" (1 Kings 19:19–21). "Fishermen who catch people" turns their trade into a mission. The prophets had used fishing as an image of judgment (Jeremiah 16:16; Amos 4:2), but here it means gathering people for God's kingdom (13:47–48).

a: they left the boat and their father
p: In a world where sons worked the family business and honored their father, this was a costly break.
b: Zebedee's family business was large enough to have hired men (Mark 1:20). For grown sons to walk away from their father and his boat broke strong expectations of honor and duty (Exodus 20:12). Jesus later makes the cost explicit: "let the dead bury their own dead" (8:21–22), and whoever loves father or mother more than him is not worthy of him (10:37). Peter will say, "We left it all behind and followed you" (19:27). James and John's mother appears later (20:20; 27:56). James was the first of the Twelve to be killed for his faith (Acts 12:2).

a: the good news of the kingdom
p: Euangelion meant joyful news, such as a victory or a new ruler. Isaiah used it for God's coming reign.
b: Euangelion is the word behind "gospel" (Old English god spel, "good story"). In the Greek world it was used for news of a victory or a ruler's birth or rise: an inscription from Priene (9 BC) calls the birthday of Augustus "the beginning of the good news for the world." In Isaiah the messenger of good news announces to Zion, "Your God is King!" (Isaiah 52:7; also Isaiah 40:9; 61:1). Matthew's "good news of the kingdom" (also 9:35; 24:14) is that announcement: God's reign has arrived in Jesus, shown in his teaching and healing.
orig: τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τῆς βασιλείας (to euangelion tēs basileias)

p: Synagogues were village meeting houses for prayer and reading Scripture. Matthew's "their" hints at a later split.
b: Synagōgē means "gathering," then the building. In first-century Galilee these were community halls where Jews met on the Sabbath to read and explain the law and the prophets; first-century synagogues have been found at Magdala and Gamla. A visiting teacher could be invited to speak (Luke 4:16–21; Acts 13:15). Matthew often writes "their synagogues" (9:35; 10:17; 12:9; 13:54), and in 23:34 "your synagogues." Many scholars think this reflects his own day, when Jesus' followers met separately and felt cut off from the synagogues around them.

p: The Greek word means "struck by the moon." The KJV says "lunatick." It describes epilepsy.
b: Selēniazomenous comes from selēnē, "moon." Many ancient people thought the moon caused seizures (compare Psalm 121:6, "or the moon in the night"). The KJV's "lunatick" (from Latin luna, moon) has come to mean madness, which misleads modern readers; many modern versions say "epileptics" or "had seizures." This translation keeps "moonstruck," here and in 17:15, so readers can see the ancient idea, and explains it here. In 17:15 the same word describes a boy with seizures whom Matthew also links to a demon. Matthew lists demon possession, seizures and paralysis separately here, so he did not treat all illness as demonic.

p: The list traces the whole land of Israel, plus the Gentile cities of the Decapolis.
b: Galilee in the north, Jerusalem and Judea in the south, and "across the Jordan" (Perea, east of the river) make up the land of Israel; Syria (4:24) lay to the north, and the Decapolis was a league of about ten Greek cities, mostly east of the Jordan (Pliny the Elder names them), with largely Gentile populations. Matthew gathers all Israel and some outsiders around Jesus, and these crowds are the hearers of the Sermon on the Mount that follows (5:1; 7:28). To "follow" here means to go after him, not yet to be a disciple.
